concept.name: Forward premium
concept.definition: The situation in which a currency's forward exchange rate is above its spot rate, i.e. the currency trades at a premium for future delivery (equivalently, positive forward points). Under covered interest parity, a currency trades at a forward premium when its interest rate is below that of the other currency in the pair.
concept.intuition: A currency at a forward premium costs more in the forward market than in the spot market — the mirror image of its lower interest rate.
concept.mechanics: With the exchange rate quoted as quote currency per base currency, positive forward points (F > S) mean the base currency is at a forward premium and the quote currency at a forward discount. The size of the premium, annualized as (F - S)/S, is tied by covered interest parity to the interest differential, plus any cross-currency basis.
concept.formula: Annualized forward premium = (F - S) / S x (360 / days to maturity); F = forward rate, S = spot rate.
concept.failure_modes: The premium is an arithmetic consequence of interest differentials and carries no information about expected appreciation; treating it as a bullish signal is an error. Basis deviations can also make the observed premium differ from the parity-implied value.
concept.misconceptions: A forward premium does not indicate that the market expects the currency to strengthen — under CIP it simply compensates for the currency's lower interest rate.
concept.example: If the yen's interest rate is below the dollar's and USD/JPY spot is 150.00 with a 1-year forward of 146.50, the dollar is at a forward discount and the yen at a forward premium of roughly 2.3% annualized.

citations.source: BIS Quarterly Review, September 2016 — Covered interest parity lost: understanding the cross-currency basis (Borio, McCauley, McGuire, Sushko)
